{{Short description|Algebraic geometry}}
In [[mathematics]], given a ''G''-[[torsor]] ''X'' → ''Y'' and a [[stack (mathematics)|stack]] ''F'', the '''descent along torsors''' says there is a canonical [[equivalence of categories|equivalence]] between ''F''(''Y''), the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of ''Y''-points and ''F''(''X'')<sup>''G''</sup>, the category of ''G''-equivariant ''X''-points.<ref>{{harvnb|Vistoli|2008|loc=Theorem 4.46}}</ref> It is a basic example of [[descent (mathematics)|descent]], since it says the "equivariant data" (which is an additional data) allows one to "descend" from ''X'' to ''Y''.

When ''G'' is the [[Galois group]] of a [[finite extension|finite]] [[Galois extension]] ''L''/''K'', for the ''G''-torsor <math>\operatorname{Spec}L \to \operatorname{Spec}K</math>, this generalizes classical '''Galois descent''' (cf. [[field of definition]]).

For example, one can take ''F'' to be the stack of quasi-coherent sheaves (in an appropriate topology). Then ''F''(''X'')<sup>''G''</sup> consists of [[equivariant sheaf|equivariant sheaves]] on ''X''; thus, the descent in this case says that to give an equivariant sheaf on ''X'' is to give a sheaf on the quotient ''X''/''G''.
